name: Silica (horsetail)

card.summary: Horsetail (Equisetum arvense), a silicon-rich herb taken as tea or extract in the hope of thicker, stronger hair and nails.
card.note: Traditional diuretic; EMA advises against use when fluid intake is restricted. Toxic to livestock.

quick.overview:
Horsetail is a plant long used in folk medicine and valued for its high silicon content. In hair and nail communities it is taken as a tea, tincture or capsule, on the idea that silica supports keratin, collagen and growth, giving thicker hair and stronger nails.

Traditional uses include skin, wound and urinary remedies, and Finnish tradition links its silicic acid to stronger skin. The EMA recognises only traditional use for minor urinary complaints and superficial wounds. Hair-specific trials of horsetail alone were not identified; some trials of combination hair supplements are registered.
quick.how: People take it as dried herb tea, liquid extract or capsules, sometimes inside multi-ingredient hair formulas, over months, since hair changes are slow. Users on looksmax.org discuss it for longer, thicker hair.
quick.risks: Reported side effects include allergic reactions and mild stomach complaints. The EMA monograph limits use to adults and adolescents over 12 and advises against urinary use where fluid reduction is medically advised. The plant is toxic to livestock, and Wikipedia notes unsourced claims of trace nicotine in polluted conditions.

lead: Horsetail (Equisetum arvense) is a primitive spore-bearing plant used in folk medicine in Austria, Finland and elsewhere for skin, joint, kidney and wound complaints; Finnish tradition prizes it for silicic acid, and it was once used to strengthen fingernails.[1] In looksmaxxing and hair-care circles it is promoted as a silica source for hair thickness and nail strength.[2]

A looksmax.org thread argues that horsetail's silica boosts scalp blood supply, hair growth and collagen.[2] The European Medicines Agency's committee recognises traditional use only for minor urinary complaints and superficial wounds and notes limited clinical data.[3]

angle.text: Users take horsetail for its silica, aiming for thicker hair and firmer nails. The hair claim is made by proponents; research on horsetail itself is mostly about traditional diuretic and wound uses.

paras: In Austria it is used as tea, bath or compress for skin, joint, kidney and urinary complaints; in Finland as a remedy for lungs and rashes; in Japan and Korea the spring buds are eaten.[1]
A forum post says silica in horsetail encourages hair growth and thickness and improves collagen production.[2]

The EMA lists allergic reactions and mild gastrointestinal complaints, limits use to those over 12, and cautions against urinary use when fluid intake is restricted.[3] It is toxic to livestock, particularly horses.[1]

A study in healthy male volunteers found a mild diuretic effect, per the EMA, with limited detail; there are no clinical studies for wounds.[3] A 2024 phase 1/2 before-after trial registered a horsetail plus palmitoylethanolamide combination for chronic pain,[4] and a registered six-month trial tests a dietary supplement for hair growth in androgenetic alopecia.[5] No published trial of horsetail alone for hair was identified.

lore.intro: Horsetail appears in hair-growth discussions on looksmax.org as a silica source.[2]

claims.claim: The silica in horsetail makes hair grow longer and thicker
claims.believers: A 2021 looksmax.org post says silica encourages growth and thickness and benefits collagen.[2]
claims.experts: The EMA recognises only traditional urinary and wound uses and cites limited clinical evidence; no hair trial of horsetail alone was found.[3]
